hook: 52 years on the water taught me one thing
script: Fifty-two years on the water taught me one thing. You can't argue with the weather. I tried. For about ten years I fought every blow that came through this bay. Went out when I shouldn't have. Lost gear. Almost lost more than gear. Then my father said, 'Walt, the ocean's not mad at you. It doesn't even know your name.' Took me a long time to hear that. Most of what's wrecking you doesn't know your name either. Haul what you can. Let the rest blow through.
caption: The ocean doesn't even know your name. 🌊

hook: I've been up at 4:30 for 60 years. Here's why.
script: I've been up at four-thirty for sixty years. People think it's discipline. It's not. It's that I stopped asking myself if I felt like it. A man who asks himself every morning if he feels like it is going to lose that argument most mornings. My father never asked. He just put his boots on. So I put my boots on. Some days the coffee's good and the water's flat. Most days it isn't. Didn't matter. The traps don't care how you feel.
caption: Stop asking yourself if you feel like it.

hook: My wife and I were married 46 years. The secret wasn't love.
script: Mary Ellen and I were married forty-six years. People ask me the secret. They want me to say love. Love's the easy part. Love shows up on its own. The secret was we never went to bed with the boat untied. Meaning whatever went wrong that day, we said it. Short. Plain. Then it was done. You leave a boat untied overnight, you wake up and it's gone. Same with a marriage. Tie it up every night.
caption: Never go to bed with the boat untied. ⚓

hook: Young guys always pull their traps too early
script: Young guys always pull their traps too early. They set 'em, come back the next morning, nothing in 'em, and they move 'em. Next day, move 'em again. Never let anything soak. Then they tell you the bay's fished out. The bay's not fished out. You just never let it work. Most good things in life need to soak. A job. A friendship. A body you're trying to fix. Set your traps somewhere smart. Then leave 'em alone.
caption: Let it soak.

hook: I never made big money. I retired fine. Here's how.
script: I never made big money. Lobstering's feast or famine. Good summer, you feel rich. Bad winter, you're eating what you saved. So I had one rule. In the good months, I lived like it was a bad month. Same truck. Same boots. Same coffee. Everybody else bought new boats in August and sold 'em in February. I'm seventy-four. Never sold my boat. Never owed a bank. You don't get rich on a good summer. You get rich surviving the winter.
caption: Live like it's a bad month. 💵

hook: My father said maybe 100 words to me a year
script: My father said maybe a hundred words to me a year. When I was a boy I thought he didn't care. Then I had my own boy. And I found out how hard it is to say the thing you mean. So you just show up. You fix the engine. You're on the dock at four-thirty. I wish I'd told him I understood before he passed. So if your old man's quiet, go sit with him. He's probably saying it the only way he knows how.
caption: Go sit with him. ❤️

hook: I almost died out there in '78. Here's what I learned.
script: February of seventy-eight. Blow came up out of nowhere. Waves over the wheelhouse. My sternman was crying. I was too, I just did it quiet. And I learned something. Fear doesn't go away when you're brave. It goes away when you're busy. I stopped thinking about dying and started thinking about the next wave. Just the next one. Then the next. We made it in. Whatever you're scared of right now, quit staring at the whole storm. Just take the next wave.
caption: Just take the next wave. 🌊

hook: Nobody's watching you work. Good.
script: Nobody watched me work for fifty-two years. Out on the bay before the sun's up, nobody's clapping. Nobody's taking pictures. Just you, the gulls, and four hundred traps. And I'll tell you, that was the best part. You find out who you are when nobody's watching. Some men only work hard with an audience. Those men don't last out here. If nobody's noticing you right now, good. That's where it gets built.
caption: That's where it gets built.

hook: My biggest regret after 74 years
script: My biggest regret isn't a bad season or a lost boat. It's all the mornings I was out on the water when Mary Ellen asked me to stay home. Just one morning, Walt. And I'd say the traps won't haul themselves. That was true. But they'd have been there tomorrow. She isn't here now. The traps are still out there. Somebody else is hauling 'em. Work will always take whatever you give it. Make sure you give some to the people at home.
caption: The traps would've been there tomorrow.

hook: Getting old isn't what scared me
script: Getting old didn't scare me. What scared me was getting useless. Bad knee took me off the boat two years ago. First month, I sat in the kitchen and stared at the wall. Then my grandson Tyler called me at five a.m. Said the engine was making a noise. I knew that noise. Fixed it over the phone. Turns out you don't stop being useful. You just stop being the one in the boat. Find where you're needed now. Somebody needs what you know.
caption: Somebody needs what you know.

hook: Stop counting the other guy's traps
script: There was a fella in this harbor who spent thirty years counting everybody else's traps. Who had the most. Who had the new boat. Who was hauling in more. Spent so much time looking at other boats he ran his own onto a ledge. Twice. You can't steer looking sideways. I don't know what the other guy's got and I don't care. I know my water. I know my traps. Keep your eyes on your own bow.
caption: You can't steer looking sideways. ⚓

hook: I started with 40 traps and a rowboat
script: I started with forty traps and a rowboat. Fourteen years old. Hauled 'em by hand. Other boys laughed. They were waiting till they could afford a real boat. Most of 'em are still waiting. Or they gave up. By the time I was twenty I had two hundred traps and a motor. By thirty I had the Mary Ellen. You don't wait till you can do it right. You do it small and you do it now. Forty traps is more than zero.
caption: Forty traps is more than zero.

hook: Grief is like the tide
script: When Mary Ellen passed, folks told me it gets easier. It doesn't get easier. It gets different. Grief's like the tide. It goes out and you think, okay, I'm fine now. Then it comes back in, and it comes in all at once. Smell of her coffee. A song on the radio. You can't stop the tide. Nobody can. But you learn the times. You learn when it's coming. And you learn it always goes back out.
caption: It always goes back out. 🌊

hook: Everybody's so loud now
script: Everybody's so loud now. Phones in every hand. Talking, talking. I spent most of my life out on the water with no noise but the engine and the birds. And I'll tell you what quiet does. It lets you hear yourself. Most people have never heard themselves think. They're scared to. Tomorrow morning, before you touch that phone, sit for ten minutes. Coffee. Window. Nothing else. You might not like what you hear. Listen anyway.
caption: Ten minutes. Coffee. Window. Nothing else. ☕

hook: On a boat, there's no one to blame
script: On a boat, there's nobody to blame. You run out of fuel, that's on you. You didn't tie off right, that's on you. Rope wraps the prop, you didn't watch your line. Took me a few years to stop blaming the weather, the gear, the price, the other guys. Once I took it all as mine, everything got better. Not because it was all my fault. Because once it's yours, you can fix it.
caption: Once it's yours, you can fix it.

hook: Pick your sternman carefully
script: Pick your sternman carefully. That's the fella who works the back of the boat with you. Twelve hours a day, close quarters, heavy gear, cold water. A bad sternman will get you hurt. Not on purpose. Just by being careless. Same thing goes on land. The people closest to you, they're either keeping you safe or getting you hurt. And they don't have to mean it either way. Look at who's in your boat.
caption: Look at who's in your boat.

hook: The best fisherman I knew asked for help
script: Best fisherman I ever knew was a man named Gus. And the thing about Gus was he asked for help more than anybody in this harbor. Where are they biting. What bait you using. Can you look at my winch. Proud men thought he was soft. Proud men caught half what Gus caught. Pride's heavy. You can't haul traps carrying it. Ask the question. Worst case, somebody thinks you don't know something. You don't. That's why you're asking.
caption: Pride's heavy. Put it down.

hook: The bay changed. Most guys didn't.
script: Water's warmer than when I started. Lobsters moved. Went deeper, went north. Half the guys in this harbor kept setting traps in the same spots their fathers did. Caught less every year and cursed the ocean. The other half followed the lobsters. Changed their gear. Learned new water. Those boats are still running. The ocean changes. Your job changes. The world changes. You can be right about how it used to be, or you can go where the lobsters went.
caption: Go where the lobsters went. 🦞

hook: We always tow each other in
script: Lot of competition in a harbor. Everybody's fighting for the same water. But I'll tell you something. In fifty-two years, I never saw a boat left out there broken down. Didn't matter if you hated the man. You towed him in. Because next week, it's you. People forget that on land. Everybody's fighting for the same water up here too. Tow 'em in anyway. Next week it's you.
caption: Next week it's you. 🚤

hook: My grandson asked me if it was worth it
script: My grandson Tyler asked me last week. Grampa, was it worth it? Fifty-two years. Cold hands. Bad back. Never got rich. I thought about it a while. Then I told him. I fed a family. I built a boat. I married a good woman. I raised your father. And now you're out there in that same boat at four-thirty in the morning. Yeah, Ty. It was worth it. It's not about what you make. It's about what you leave running.
caption: It's about what you leave running. ⚓
